prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Coyote scruff in canyons off Mulholland Drive. Fragrance of sage and rosemary, now it’s spring. At night the mockingbirds ring their warnings of cats coming across the neighborhoods. Like castanets in the palms of a dancer, the palm trees clack. The HOLLYWOOD sign has a white skin of fog across it where erotic canyons hump, moisten, slide, dry up, swell, and shift. They appear impatient—to make such powerful contact with pleasure that they will toss back the entire cover of earth. She walks for days around brown trails, threading sometimes under the low branches of bay and acacia. Bitter flowers will catch her eye: pink and thin honeysuckle, or mock orange. They coat the branches like lace in the back of a mystical store. Other deviant men and women live at the base of these canyons, closer to the city however. Her mouth is often dry, her chest tight, but she is filled to the brim with excess idolatry. It was like a flat mouse—the whole of Los Angeles she could hold in the circle formed by her thumb and forefinger. Tires were planted to stop the flow of mud at her feet. But she could see all the way to Long Beach through a tunnel made in her fist. Her quest for the perfect place was only a symptom of the same infection that was out there, a mild one, but a symptom nonetheless.

outputs.L3:
The canyons off Mulholland Drive are alive with the sensory details of nature. The air carries the pungent scent of sage and rosemary, herbs that grow wild along the ridges and release their fragrance in the heat. Overhead, the palm trees clack their dry fronds together in the wind, a sound like distant applause, while mockingbirds fill the silences with their warning calls, sharp and territorial against the hush of the hills.

The landscape reveals itself in vividly erotic and restless terms. The Hollywood sign sits half-shrouded in fog, its famous letters softened and made strange by the mist, and the canyons themselves seem to strain with impatience, as if aching to make some powerful, physical contact with pleasure. There is a tension in the scenery, a coiled energy that refuses to settle into mere postcard beauty.

She wanders for days along the brown trails that thread through this terrain, taking careful note of what grows there. Bitter flowers—honeysuckle and mock orange—coat the branches like lace, their delicate white blossoms belying the sharpness of their scent. The trails wind on, dusty and endless, and she follows them without any clear destination.

Despite her physical discomfort—the dryness of her mouth, the tightness gripping her chest—she is consumed by an excess of idolatry as she surveys the vast sprawl of Los Angeles below. The city stretches out beyond measure, and she cannot help but worship it, even as her body registers its quiet protest against the heat and the exertion and the longing.

Yet her search for the perfect place is ultimately revealed to be something more troubling than simple desire. It is a symptom, a sign of the same underlying infection that pervades the city all around her—a restless, insatiable yearning that she has not escaped by climbing into the hills, but has only carried with her, breathing it in with every fragrant, feverish breath.
outputs.L4:
She walks the brown trails that thread through the canyons off Mulholland Drive, where the earth cracks and crumbles beneath her feet, releasing the dusty scent of the season. The air here is thick with fragrance—sage and eucalyptus, the peppery sweetness of wild fennel, the resinous perfume of chaparral baking under a relentless sun. She breathes it in, letting it settle into her lungs, and for a moment she is nothing but a body moving through the landscape, alive to every sensation.

The canyons are wilder than the city they overlook. A hawk carves slow circles overhead. Somewhere in the underbrush a rustle betrays a lizard, a rabbit, some small creature going about its secret business. The hills themselves seem to have a body of their own—soft folds and sudden hollows, sun-warmed slopes and shadowed crevices, an eroticized geography that presses against her awareness. She feels the sweat gathering at the small of her back, the pull of muscle in her calves, the sun laying its heat across her shoulders like a hand.

From the ridgeline she stops and looks down. Los Angeles unfurls below her, an endless grid of pale streets and glinting glass fading into the brown haze of the horizon. It is vast, ungraspable, a city that seems to have no edges and no center. And yet she raises her hand, holds it up against the distance, and finds she can cover it all—the towers, the freeways, the numberless houses—beneath the span of her palm. The whole sprawling monster reduced to something she can hold, contain, possess. It gives her a strange and fleeting satisfaction, this illusion of mastery.

But she does not stay. She never stays. She is looking for something—she has always been looking. The perfect place, she tells herself, the exact spot where the view opens just so, where the light falls right, where she might finally feel that she has arrived. She wanders on, one trail giving way to the next, each promising more than it delivers. Her yearning feels intimate, hers alone, a private restlessness that drives her up into these hills and keeps her circling.

Yet the longer she searches, the more she comes to understand that her longing is not hers alone. This need to keep moving, to keep looking, to believe that fulfillment waits just over the next ridge—it is everywhere. It rises from the city below like heat off the pavement. It is written in the endless sprawl itself, in the way Los Angeles pushes always outward, never satisfied, never complete. Her private hunger is only a single symptom of a larger condition, an infection that has spread through the whole basin and everyone in it. What she thought was her own restlessness is in fact the city's own fever, shared and inescapable—a malaise she carries not because she is different, but because she belongs.
outputs.L5:
# Coyote on Mulholland Drive

The coyote appeared like a ghost at the edge of Mulholland Drive, its silver-gray coat catching the last amber light of a Los Angeles sunset. Along this famous ridge road that snakes across the Santa Monica Mountains, encounters between wildlife and the sprawling city below are more common than most people realize.

## Where Wilderness Meets the City

Mulholland Drive has long symbolized the strange intersection of glamour and wilderness that defines Los Angeles. Named after William Mulholland, the engineer who brought water to the growing metropolis, this winding road offers breathtaking views of both the San Fernando Valley and the Los Angeles Basin. Yet just beyond the luxury homes and scenic overlooks lies genuine wild country.

The coyote is perhaps the most successful native predator to adapt to this urban-wild boundary. Unlike many species that retreated as the city expanded, coyotes learned to thrive in the margins, patrolling the canyons and ridgelines that humans have not completely claimed.

## A Survivor's Story

What makes the coyote so remarkable is its intelligence and adaptability. These animals hunt rabbits, rodents, and other small prey in the chaparral-covered hillsides, but they have also learned to navigate the dangers of roads, fences, and human activity. On quiet nights, their haunting calls echo across the canyons, a reminder that the wild has never truly left the city.

For drivers traveling Mulholland after dark, catching a glimpse of a coyote crossing the road is a moment of unexpected connection—a brush with something ancient and untamed in the heart of modern civilization.

## Living Together

As Los Angeles continues to grow, the relationship between residents and coyotes remains complicated. These clever survivors remind us that even in one of the world's largest cities, nature persists, adapts, and endures—right there along the curves of Mulholland Drive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, sensory prose passage about a woman wandering the canyons and trails above Los Angeles near Mulholland Drive, blending descriptions of nature with themes of desire, obsession, and searching for the perfect place.
counterfactuals.output:
She walks the fire roads at the hour when the city below begins to shed its daylight skin, when the smog goes rose and violet and the whole basin exhales its heat upward toward her. The chaparral is dry as an old letter. She trails her fingers through the wild fennel and brings them to her face, breathing that green anise sharpness, and thinks: *this, this is close, but not yet the place.*

She is always searching for the place.

The trails fork and double back on themselves like the folds of some enormous sleeping thing, and she follows them past the ruins of houses that burned decades ago—a lone chimney standing in the sage, a set of steps that climb to nothing, a swimming pool cracked and filled with dead leaves and the small bones of animals. She lingers there. She imagines the parties that must have happened, the bodies moving through blue underwater light, the laughter that has long since evaporated into this same air she is breathing now. Desire has a half-life, she thinks. It leaves a residue on everything.

The sun goes down and the coyotes begin their thin electric keening from the next ridge over, and she does not hurry. She wants to be caught out here. She wants the dark to find her still climbing, still certain that just around the next switchback the land will open into exactly the vista she has been aching toward her whole life—some overlook where the city lays itself down entirely, offered, a bowl of trembling light she could cup in her two hands.

She has been up here a hundred times. She knows this is a form of madness, this returning, this belief that a place can save you, can hold whatever it is you cannot name in yourself. The manzanita snags her sleeve like a hand asking her to stay. Below her the reservoir catches the last of the light and holds it, a coin of mercury pressed into the dark hills.

Somewhere down there is everyone who ever wanted something. The whole city is nothing but wanting, ten million appetites glittering in the smog, and she is part of it, she is the wanting made flesh and given legs and sent up into the hills to walk it off, to walk toward it, she can no longer tell which.

The perfect place. She almost has its shape now. It is always just ahead, where the trail dissolves into blue evening, where the last house before the wildness has left one window lit—and she moves toward that gold rectangle the way a moth moves, the way water moves downhill, helpless and deliberate at once, certain only that the thing she is looking for looks exactly like arrival, and that she will know it, finally, when the ground beneath her feet says *here, stop, you are home.*

She does not stop. The dark comes down over the canyons like a lid, and still she climbs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of experimental literary fiction set in the Hollywood Hills that uses eroticized imagery of the landscape and describes a restless female character's spiritual quest amid the city.
counterfactuals.output:
# Topography of Wanting

The hills are a body she has never learned to read.

Mara walks them at the hour when light goes amber and thick as poured honey, when the canyon's flank rises golden and dry-grassed, the fire roads cutting their pale seams across the swell of earth. She has lived here eight months and still she cannot say what she is looking for. Only that she is looking. That the looking has become the thing itself.

The land here does not lie flat and honest. It heaves. It folds into itself, ravine and ridge, the chaparral clinging to slopes that curve like the inside of a wrist, the secret undersides of things. In the mornings the fog settles into the low places and she thinks: *there, the hollows where the water would go if there were water.* There is no water. There is only the wanting of it, the dry riverbed of Mara's own attention scouring the hills for something to fill her.

---

She came west the way people have always come west, believing the geography would do the work. As if a place could be a prayer. As if you could stand on a hillside and let the whole basin of the city open below you—that trembling grid of light, that vast lit circuitry breathing its sodium glow into the dark—and feel yourself *arrive.*

But arrival is not a thing that happens to you. She is learning this slowly, the way you learn the weather of a new country: through error, through exposure.

At night the city is an offering laid out beneath her. She stands at the overlook and the lights pulse, a million small ignitions, and she feels the old ache rise—the one that has followed her from the flat gray middle of the country, the ache that says *more, elsewhere, next.* The hills receive this ache. They are shaped for it. Every ridgeline promises another ridgeline beyond it, another fold of golden flesh, another crest to be topped and found insufficient.

She has begun to suspect that the promise is the whole point. That the landscape seduces precisely because it never delivers. The eye is drawn up the slope and over and there is always more slope, more distance, the horizon receding like a lover who will not be caught, only pursued.

---

There is a coyote that crosses her path some evenings. It regards her without fear, without interest, a lean gray fact of the hills. She envies it terribly. It wants only what the hills contain—the rabbit, the shade, the going-on. It does not stand at the overlook manufacturing longing. It is not sick with the disease of the sublime.

*Teach me,* she says to it once, aloud, and feels foolish, and the coyote is already gone, folded back into the brush, into the body of the hill that opens and closes around it like water around a swimmer.

---

She reads, at night, in the little rented room with its window full of hillside. She reads the desert mystics, the ones who went out into dry places to be emptied. She underlines: *The soul is a country with no roads.* She thinks this is beautiful and then she thinks it is a lie, because the hills are full of roads, fire roads and switchbacks and the private drives snaking up to houses cantilevered over the drop, all that human wanting made structural, made to hang above the abyss on steel and nerve.

Maybe that is the American version. Not to empty yourself in the desert but to build a glass house on the edge of the wanting and live there, suspended, looking out.

---

One evening she climbs higher than she has gone before. The trail narrows. The city drops away behind her and for a while there is only the hill and the sky and the sound of her own breath, which is the sound of a body doing the simplest work of staying alive.

The sun is going down into the ocean she cannot see but knows is there, westward, always westward, the final edge of the continent where all the wanting piles up against the water and has nowhere left to go. The light comes low and horizontal and turns the grass to filament, to fire, each dry blade lit from within. The slope before her glows. It is almost unbearable, the beauty—the way the whole hillside seems to arch toward the light, to lift and offer itself.

And Mara stops.

She stops and she does not climb the next ridge.

She sits down in the burning grass and she lets the wanting move through her like weather, and she does not chase it up the hill. She watches it come and she watches it go. The ache rises and she lets it rise. It crests and she lets it crest. And on the other side of it—this is the thing she has come all this way to learn, though she did not know it—on the other side of it there is just the hill, just the light, just the enormous indifferent tenderness of a place that was never hiding anything from her at all.

The city begins its slow ignition below. One light, then a hundred, then the whole trembling field of them.

She does not need to go down to it yet.

She sits in the last of the sun on the body of the hill, and for one held breath she is not looking for anything.

She is only, finally, *here*—

which turns out to be the country with no roads,

which turns out to have been under her the whole time,

golden, and dry, and waiting to be walked upon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, poetic paragraph capturing the atmosphere of the canyons off Mulholland Drive in spring—sage, mockingbirds, palm trees, fog on the Hollywood sign—and a solitary woman's yearning as she looks down over the whole of LA.
counterfactuals.output: Spring loosens itself along Mulholland in a slow exhale of sage and eucalyptus, the hillsides silvered green after rain, and she stands where the road bends into nothing, one woman held between the canyon's throat and the vast indifferent sprawl below. Mockingbirds run their borrowed songs through the cool morning—a dozen voices in one small gray body, none of them its own—and she listens as if the trick might teach her something about wanting. Palm trees lift their ragged crowns above the fog that pools in the low places, and across the ridge the Hollywood sign floats half-erased, its letters surfacing and dissolving like a promise she can neither read nor forget. Beneath her the city unspools to the sea, a million windows catching the thin light, each one a life she is not living, and the yearning comes up in her like the marine layer itself—soft, formless, filling the hollows—not for any single thing she could name, but for the whole shimmering impossible reach of it, the distance that is also, she understands, a kind of tenderness: the way a place can hold you and never once look back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of Joan Didion or a similar California writer, describe a woman hiking the brown trails of the Los Angeles canyons who becomes obsessed with finding a perfect place, weaving in sensory detail and a sense of underlying sickness or infection.
counterfactuals.output:
She began hiking Fryman Canyon in the dry months, when the trails had gone the color of old bone and the chaparral gave off that smell—sage and dust and something underneath it, something faintly sweet, the way a thing smells when it is turning. She told herself she was walking for her health. This is what women in Los Angeles tell themselves. They lace up their shoes and climb into the hills as though altitude were a form of absolution, as though the city below, laid out flat and shimmering in its own exhaust, were a thing you could leave.

What she was looking for, though she would not have said so, was a place.

Not a house. A place. A specific configuration of light and stone and silence that she believed existed somewhere along these ridges, a spot where she would stand and feel, finally, that she had arrived. She had felt it once, briefly, at a switchback near the top where the trail opened and the whole basin fell away beneath her and the eucalyptus threw down their long medicinal shadows. For a moment the feeling had come—clean, total—and then it was gone, and she spent the next many mornings trying to find it again.

The canyons do not give things back. This is what people who love them refuse to understand.

She walked earlier and earlier. By August she was on the trail before six, when the coyotes were still moving and the marine layer sat low and gray over the ridgelines like something that had settled on a wound. Her legs grew hard. Her face grew thin. She learned the trails the way you learn a lover's failures—the loose scree below the water tower, the place where the poison oak came up red and glossy and beautiful, the fire road that dead-ended at nothing, at a chain-link fence and a view of somebody's pool.

The perfect place kept receding. Each turn promised it. Each ridge withheld it.

She noticed, that summer, a scratch on her ankle that would not close. She had gotten it on the manzanita, or the yucca, or something with a thorn, she could not remember, and it had gone a dull pink at the edges and then a deeper color, and it wept a little in the heat. She did not stop walking. She wrapped it and walked. The trails by then had a smell she could not name, or would not, the smell of things drying out and things going soft at the same time, the two processes that in California are never as separate as you would like.

There is a sickness in wanting a place too much. Anyone who has lived here long enough knows it, the way you can love a landscape until it becomes a kind of fever, until the wanting is indistinguishable from the loss. She walked to feel well and grew unwell in the walking. The canyon took her mornings and her weight and the color from her face and gave her, in exchange, the promise—always the promise, never the thing—of a place just past the next brown rise where she might finally lie down.

By September the ankle had gone the gray-green of the sage. She barely noticed. She was looking at the ridgeline, at the one gold notch of light where she was almost certain, this time, the perfect place would be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness literary excerpt about Los Angeles seen from the hills, mixing wild flora, animals, the built environment, and a character's inner longing and idolatry.
counterfactuals.output:
From up here the city lies flat and shimmering, a spilled tray of light, and Marisol crouches among the sagebrush with her knees pressed into the dry crumbling dirt, the smell of it—that peppery green resin of chaparral, black sage and California buckwheat gone to rust—rising up around her like incense, like the smoke of some altar she has built without meaning to, because isn't that what she does, isn't that always what she does, builds altars, kneels before things too far away to touch.

A coyote crosses the fire road below her, unhurried, its coat the exact tawny nothing-color of the hillside so that it seems less an animal than a piece of the land loosening itself, ambling down toward the sprinklers and swimming pools and the blue rectangles of other people's afternoons. She envies it. She envies the way it wants only water, only the next warm body of a rabbit trembling in the wild oats, envies its clean uncomplicated hunger, while hers is all tangled up in a face on a billboard—*his* face, thirty feet of it grinning over Sunset, teeth like the white curve of the moon, and she has driven past it eleven times this week just to feel the swoop in her chest, the terrible sweet sick swoop.

The wind comes up off the basin carrying jet-fuel and jasmine and the sound of a leaf blower somewhere, always somewhere, the eternal drone of maintenance, and below her the city grids itself out into perfect indifference—the towers downtown catching the last copper light like ingots, the freeways pulsing their red and white corpuscles, and she thinks *I could be any of those lights, I am none of them, I am up here with the lizards.* A fence lizard does its little push-ups on the granite outcrop, blue-bellied, ancient, doing its small proud dominion dance for no one, and a red-tailed hawk turns overhead on a thermal, and yarrow nods, and a hummingbird—Anna's, iridescent gorget flaring pink then black then pink—stitches the air by the monkeyflower, and none of it, none of it knows his name.

She whispers it anyway. She has made a religion of a stranger. She has taken a man she watched flicker across a screen in a dark theater and she has enshrined him up here in the coyote-brush and the wild cucumber vine, has laid him among the poppies that close their orange fists at dusk, and she knows—she *knows*—that he is at this very moment somewhere down in that grid, in some house behind a gate, eating dinner, laughing, being unimaginably real, being nobody's god, being only a man with a headache maybe, with bills, with a dog. And that is the cruelty of it, that longing points always at the wrong distance, that she can see the whole city and hold none of it, that the manzanita's smooth red limbs are more truly hers than any dream she polishes in the dark.

The light goes. The city does its trick, its magic hour to full electric blaze, ten thousand windows lighting one by one like the offerings of some congregation she is not part of, and the coyote is gone now, folded back into the hill, and the sage exhales its last warmth, and Marisol stays, kneeling, faithful, ridiculous, in love with an idea, in love with a face, in love—she suspects, and hates that she suspects it—only with the ache itself, with this high wild place where she can want everything and be asked for nothing, where the whole glittering unreachable body of Los Angeles lies below her like something worshipped, like something that will never, ever turn its head.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
